query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Co-doping a refractory high-entropy alloy with trace amounts of Yttrium (Y) and Hafnium (Hf) improves its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent, and slowly growing alumina-rich oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based) without any reactive element doping.
generation.intervention: Introduce Y and Hf dopants into the alloy (for example, via laser cladding to create a thin doped surface layer) to serve as reactive elements at the oxide/metal interface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high temperatures (approximately 900 °C) in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (such as air or pure O2) for extended periods (around 10 hours) under static conditions; minor salt impurities may be present to mimic realistic service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The dopants (Y and Hf) segregate to grain boundaries during oxidation, facilitating the formation of an Al-rich (alumina) layer that is more continuous and less prone to spallation.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf act as reactive elements that enhance the adhesion and integrity of the growing alumina oxide scale by reducing growth stresses and healing interface defects. This results in a more protective, slowly growing oxide that resists further oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Y/Hf co-doped alloy will exhibit reduced oxidation damage (as evidenced by lower mass gain, thinner and more uniform oxide scale, and less scale spallation) when exposed to 900 °C in an oxygen-rich environment.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exposed under identical temperature, atmosphere, and duration conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is predicted under the specified conditions (∼900 °C, oxygen-rich atmosphere, and 10-hour exposure). The improvement might vary under different thermal cycles, higher temperatures, or severe mechanical stresses.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant concentration and the precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance are not yet determined. Furthermore, the long-term behavior under cyclic thermal stresses remains to be tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using a refractory high-entropy alloy: one set with a surface layer co-doped with Y and Hf (applied via laser cladding) and the other set without doping. Expose both sets to an oxygen-rich environment at 900 °C for 10 hours.
measurements: Mass gain after exposure to quantify oxidation extent
SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy) analysis of surface morphology and oxide scale continuity
Cross-sectional analysis to measure oxide scale thickness and continuity
Spallation or adhesion tests to assess oxide scale integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in mass gain, thinner and more uniform oxide scales, and improved scale adhesion compared to the undoped samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, the Y and Hf co-doping did not change the microstructure morphology and phase structure of the coatings but did improve the thermal stability and resistance of the hot corrosion oxide scale spallation, providing a certain amount of data and theoretical support for the application of EHEA coat
